title: What do you want? (Luke 18:31–43)
hook: a blind beggar at Jericho shouts, and Jesus stops the whole procession

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich ruler, the one thing he lacked, and a Needle's Eye gate with no evidence behind it. Your line was what is impossible with men.

Just before Jericho, Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them plainly what's coming in Jerusalem: he'll be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, killed, and on the third day rise again. And Luke adds an almost sad sentence: "And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." They have eyes. They've seen everything. And they can't see. Then, outside Jericho, they meet a man who has no eyesight at all.

Luke doesn't name him; Mark calls him Bartimaeus. He's begging by the roadside, hears a crowd, and asks what's happening. Jesus of Nazareth is passing. And he shouts, in the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David is a title for the promised king. The man who can't see is the one who sees who Jesus is. The people at the front tell him to be quiet. "But he cried so much the more." Then: "And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him." A whole crowd on the road to Jerusalem, and it stops for one beggar. Then a question that sounds too obvious: "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?" Jesus asks anyway, letting the man say it himself, as a person with a voice and not just a problem. "Lord, that I may receive my sight." The Greek verb can mean see again, and it can mean look up. "And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God." Up the road to Jerusalem, toward everything the disciples couldn't understand. Look at the week: a beggar with a name, faith the size of a seed, one who turned back to give thanks, a kingdom in your midst, babies carried forward, a ruler who couldn't let go. And now a blind man who could see, a shout that stopped a crowd, and a question: what do you want?
screen: `SON OF DAVID: HE SEES WHO HE IS.`
then, large: `LORD, THAT I MAY RECEIVE MY SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of the voices around you asking for help, some loud, some quiet: a friend who keeps mentioning a hard time, a family member who calls too often. Imagine your day halting the way the crowd did, and asking one of them: what do you want me to do for you? Listen for their answer, not yours, and if you pray, ask for eyes to see who's calling.
Bartimaeus, the blind beggar outside Jericho, unnamed in Luke and named by Mark, whose shout stopped a whole crowd.
Your line: Jesus stood still. One voice was enough to stop him. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week on the path.

screen: `DAY 567 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SALVATION CAME TO THIS HOUSE.`

howItsDone: Some Christians hear the blind man's cry, have mercy on me, in the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox Christians and others repeat, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; the story is also read when praying for healing and for spiritual sight.

He didn't know the man was blind until he heard him ask for sight.

chat.meaning: Jesus stood still and asked, what wilt thou? He let the man speak for himself: Lord, that I may receive my sight.

Bartimaeus.meaning: Mark's name for the blind beggar near Jericho

Jericho.meaning: the town where Jesus meets the blind beggar

son of David.meaning: a title for the promised king

Gentiles.meaning: non-Jewish peoples; those Jesus says he'll be handed to

notes: Carry 'jesus stood still' is the index line (lowercase as given); 'stood still' is Mark 10:49 KJV. Luke 18:40 KJV says 'Jesus stood'. The carry is kept exactly; the spoken carry capitalizes Jesus.
ἀναβλέπω: 'regain sight' and 'look up': standard lexicon. Confirm form ἀναβλέψω.
Year one (day 205, Bartimaeus) used Mark's version and the question 'what do you want?'; this day centers Luke's pairing with 18:34 and 'Jesus stood'.
The Jesus Prayer's link to Luke 18:38 and 18:13: commonly cited. Confirm.
